about: Annotated reading list shown on reading.html. Each reading appears under every theme in its themes list. start_here.order places it among the Start here cards. url fields are picked up by scripts/source_links.py for archiving and the monthly link check.

themes.heading: What counts as a shortage?
themes.question: Why claims about 'teacher shortages' differ so much, and what to ask of any shortage figure.

themes.heading: How many school positions go unfilled?
themes.question: Studies that measure unfilled positions directly, and how vacancies vary across schools, positions and places.

themes.heading: Beyond teachers
themes.question: Administrators, paraprofessionals, and other school staff, who make up about half of the school workforce but are much less studied.

themes.heading: Schools and the wider labor market
themes.question: How shortages, teacher entry and exit, and who chooses teaching move with the economy and with opportunities outside schools, and how schools compare with other employers.
themes.dashboard_label: Education and the whole labor market since 2000
themes.note: Teacher turnover figures here are annual and defined differently across studies, so they are not directly comparable with each other or with the dashboard's monthly JOLTS quit rates.

themes.heading: How large is the school workforce, and why has it grown?
themes.question: Long-run growth in staff relative to enrollment, and the role of pandemic relief funds.

themes.heading: Who enters, leaves, and returns?
themes.question: The pipeline into teaching, exits from it, and why fewer new licenses need not mean fewer teachers.

themes.heading: The pandemic period
themes.question: What happened to school staffing during and after COVID-19, compared with other workers.
themes.dashboard_label: Education and the whole labor market since 2000
themes.note: These studies define turnover differently. Some count only teachers who leave the state's teaching workforce; others also count moves to another school or into non-teaching roles. Their rates are not comparable with each other, or with the monthly JOLTS quit rates on the dashboard.

themes.heading: What helps fill hard-to-staff positions?
themes.question: Evidence on compensation and targeted incentives, which most consistently show effects on recruitment and retention.

readings.authors: Bruno, P.
readings.title: Figuring out when to panic about “teacher shortages”: How journalism could clarify stories about teacher hiring problems
readings.note: A short, practical guide to reading shortage stories: define what is in short supply, ask which positions are hard to fill, look for consequences for students, and compare schools with the rest of the economy. The questions the dashboard is built around.

start_here.why: Shortest; the dashboard's framing in brief.

readings.authors: Cowan, J., Goldhaber, D., Hayes, K., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: Missing elements in the discussion of teacher shortages
readings.note: Using the historical data available in 2016, the authors show that production of new teacher candidates had risen steadily since the mid-1980s and that only about half were hired as public school teachers in a typical year, so aggregate supply was a poor guide to shortages. Shortages were real but concentrated in particular subjects, such as STEM and special education, and in disadvantaged schools.

readings.authors: Nguyen, T. D., Lam, C. B., & Bruno, P.
readings.title: What do we know about the extent of teacher shortages nationwide? A systematic examination of reports of U.S. teacher shortages
readings.note: Compiles state vacancy reports, agency data and correspondence: about 1.8% of teaching positions vacant across states with data, and a little over 9% held by teachers without full licensure. Data were uneven, and about a quarter of states had none.

start_here.why: The closest thing to a national vacancy estimate.
start_here.title: What do we know about the extent of teacher shortages nationwide?

readings.authors: Bruno, P.
readings.title: Pandemic-era school staff shortages: Evidence from unfilled position data in Illinois
readings.note: Uses Illinois's unfilled-position data for fall 2022: 2.6% of teacher positions and 0.9% of administrator positions were unfilled, compared with 5.6% for other certificated staff, mostly paraprofessionals. Half of districts reported no unfilled teaching positions, and shortages varied substantially between schools within districts.

start_here.why: The Illinois data on the dashboard, in depth.

readings.authors: Bruno, P.
readings.title: Teacher supply and turnover
readings.venue: In D. Harris (Ed.), Live Handbook of Education Policy Research. Association for Education Finance and Policy. Last updated March 2026
readings.note: A synthesis of the evidence: the teacher workforce has grown much faster than enrollment; measured vacancy rates are low, generally 1–4%, and lower than economy-wide rates; shortages are concentrated in certain schools and positions; exits rise when unemployment is low; and targeted pay raises recruitment and retention.

start_here.why: Longest; the evidence behind most of this list.
start_here.venue: Live Handbook of Education Policy Research

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: Sorting out the issues in the teacher shortage crisis
readings.note: Argues that a prominent projection of a national shortage was likely wrong: it conflated supply with demand and was highly sensitive to assumptions such as future pupil-teacher ratios. The real problems are long-standing ones in particular subjects and schools.

readings.authors: Edwards, D. S., Kraft, M. A., Christian, A., & Candelaria, C. A.
readings.title: Teacher shortages: A framework for understanding and predicting vacancies
readings.note: Offers a framework for thinking about vacancies and applies it to a survey of Tennessee administrators: under 2% of teaching positions were unfilled at the start of 2019–20, with higher rates in schools serving more Black students. In a separate district survey, districts most often reported too few applicants in math, science, foreign language and special education.

start_here.why: Why statewide vacancy rates can hide shortages concentrated in particular schools.
start_here.title: Teacher shortages: A framework for understanding and predicting vacancies

readings.authors: Wyckoff, J.
readings.title: Teacher salaries, a policy brief
readings.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 43(3), 944–953
readings.note: Uses Virginia data to show that schools with concentrations of poor students have substantially more teaching vacancies, and that lower starting salaries are associated with more vacancies. Recommends raising salaries generally, with larger increases for effective teachers in high-poverty schools and shortage subjects such as special education, math and science.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., Falken, G. T., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: What do teacher job postings tell us about school hiring needs and equity?
readings.note: Uses job postings, validated against eventual hires, to show that schools serving more students of color had greater hiring needs throughout the year, and that needs were considerably higher for special education and STEM positions than for elementary ones. Postings measure hiring needs rather than unfilled positions.

readings.authors: Engel, M., Jacob, B. A., & Curran, F. C.
readings.title: New evidence on teacher labor supply
readings.note: At Chicago teacher job fairs, the number of applicants per school ranged from under five to over 300. Schools serving more advantaged students drew more applicants per vacancy, and location strongly predicted applications. A reminder that applicant numbers and vacancies are different things.

readings.authors: Bruno, P.
readings.title: We need to talk about how we compensate school staff
readings.venue: Journal of Education Finance and Law, 50(1), 212–224
readings.note: Identifies five often-neglected choices in compensating school staff, beginning with the choice to hire more staff rather than pay staff more, and their implications for recruiting and retaining staff.

readings.authors: Yang, M., Lee, S. W., & Goff, P. T.
readings.title: Labor dynamics of school principals in rural contexts
readings.note: Wisconsin job-opening and application data show rural districts received about as many applications for principal positions as urban ones, but higher-poverty rural districts received fewer, and women and candidates of color were less likely to apply to rural districts.

readings.authors: Theobald, R., Kaler, L., Bettini, E., & Jones, N.
readings.title: A descriptive portrait of the paraeducator workforce in Washington State
readings.note: Twenty-five years of statewide data on paraeducators, who make up most of Illinois's unfilled non-teaching certificated positions. Their full-time salaries are about half those of special education teachers, and their attrition from the workforce rose from 8% after 2008–09 to 23% after 2021–22.

readings.authors: Kraft, M. A., Conklin, M. L., & Falken, G. T.
readings.title: Preferences, inequities, and incentives in the substitute teacher labor market
readings.note: In Chicago, bonuses for substitutes working in largely segregated Black schools with historically low coverage of teacher absences substantially improved coverage and raised student achievement. The authors estimate incentives would need to be about half of daily wages to close coverage gaps. Relevant because some unfilled positions, including Illinois's, are covered by substitutes.

readings.authors: Pounder, D. G., Galvin, P., & Shepherd, P.
readings.title: An analysis of the United States educational administrator shortage
readings.note: Examines why an administrator shortage was widely perceived despite questionable evidence, pointing to the complexity of supply and demand data, over-generalization, and anecdotes about candidate quality standing in for evidence on candidate numbers.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: Teacher attrition and mobility over time
readings.note: Thirty-five years of Washington data: between 5% and 8% of teachers left the workforce each year, with a strong negative relationship between attrition and the state unemployment rate.

readings.authors: Falch, T., Johansen, K., & Strøm, B.
readings.title: Teacher shortages and the business cycle
readings.note: Using Norwegian municipalities from 1981 to 2002, where a centralized pay system holds teacher wages fixed, finds shortages rise when regional unemployment falls. Shortages are measured as the share of teachers without approved qualifications, not unfilled positions.

readings.authors: Nagler, M., Piopiunik, M., & West, M. R.
readings.title: Weak markets, strong teachers: Recession at career start and teacher effectiveness
readings.note: Among 33,000 Florida teachers, those who entered teaching during recessions were more effective at raising test scores, consistent with weaker outside options drawing stronger candidates.

readings.authors: Harris, D. N., & Adams, S. J.
readings.title: Understanding the level and causes of teacher turnover: A comparison with other professions
readings.note: Using Current Population Survey data, finds teachers' average turnover is not significantly higher than that of nurses, social workers, or accountants. Teachers differ mainly in higher turnover among older workers, which the authors link to earlier retirement and the generosity of pensions relative to salaries.

readings.authors: Bleiberg, J. F., & Kraft, M. A.
readings.title: What happened to the K–12 education labor market during COVID? The acute need for better data systems
readings.note: Combines BLS and state data: K–12 employment fell 9% at the onset of the pandemic and remained below pre-pandemic levels two years later, while teacher turnover dipped and then returned to pre-pandemic levels. Points to weak hiring and high attrition among support and non-instructional staff, and argues for better national data.

readings.authors: Aldeman, C.
readings.title: New employment data: 5 things to know about the state of the education workforce
readings.note: A readable tour of BLS and Census data much like the dashboard's: public education had the lowest job-opening rate of any major industry, employment losses were concentrated among part-time staff, and full-time-equivalent staffing was above pre-pandemic levels.

start_here.why: How education compares with other industries, using the same federal data as the dashboard.
start_here.title: New employment data: 5 things to know about the state of the education workforce

readings.authors: Hobijn, B.
readings.title: “Great resignations” are common during fast recoveries
readings.venue: FRBSF Economic Letter 2022-08, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, April 4
readings.note: On the broader recovery: the record U.S. quit rate of late 2021 resembled quit waves during earlier fast recoveries, was concentrated among younger and less-educated workers in hard-hit industries such as retail and food service, and rarely involved a change of occupation. The letter does not examine schools. For education it offers a benchmark rather than an explanation: rising quits are common in fast recoveries, but whether the same forces drove quits in schools is not something the letter tests.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., Falken, G., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: ESSER funding and school system jobs: Evidence from job posting data
readings.note: Using Washington job postings from 2022 to 2024, finds pandemic relief (ESSER) funding significantly increased teacher hiring, especially in its early years. Relevant to whether some post-pandemic hiring difficulty reflected new positions rather than lost staff.

readings.authors: Aldeman, C.
readings.title: Where are all the special educators?
readings.note: From 1999–2000 to 2020–21, special education teachers increased 59% while students receiving special education services increased 16%. Argues that growing demand, not just weak supply, accounts for much of the persistent shortage of special educators.

readings.authors: Kraft, M. A., & Lyon, M. A.
readings.title: The rise and fall of the teaching profession: Prestige, interest, preparation, and satisfaction over the last half century
readings.note: Fifty years of national data on the profession's prestige, students' interest, numbers preparing to teach, and job satisfaction show a common pattern: a decline in the 1970s, a rise into the mid-1990s, and a sustained decline since about 2010 to at or near the lowest levels in 50 years.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., Krieg, J., Theobald, R., & Liddle, S.
readings.title: Lost to the system? A descriptive exploration of teacher candidates' career paths
readings.note: About two-thirds of more than 14,000 recent Washington teacher candidates taught in public schools within five years. Candidates who graduated after the Great Recession were far more likely to be teaching.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., Krieg, J. M., Liddle, S., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: Out of the gate, but not necessarily teaching: A descriptive portrait of early career earnings for those who are credentialed to teach
readings.note: Credentialed candidates who did not become teachers generally earned less than those who did, which the authors read as consistent with limits on teacher hiring rather than candidates being drawn away by better pay.

readings.authors: Bartanen, B., Avitabile, A., & Kwok, A.
readings.title: Who wants to be a teacher in America?
readings.venue: EdWorkingPaper 25-1275, Annenberg Institute at Brown University
readings.note: Among 11.5 million college applicants from 2014 to 2025, interest in teaching and other lower-wage helping careers fell by about a fifth over the decade, while interest in nursing rose sharply.

readings.authors: Goldhaber, D., & Theobald, R.
readings.title: Teacher attrition and mobility in the pandemic
readings.note: Washington's teacher attrition rose from 6.4% after 2019–20 to 7.3% after 2020–21, within the range of pre-pandemic years, and gaps in turnover between high- and low-poverty classrooms narrowed.

readings.authors: Bacher-Hicks, A., Chi, O. L., & Orellana, A.
readings.title: Two years later: How COVID-19 has shaped the teacher workforce
readings.note: In Massachusetts, teacher turnover going into fall 2020 was similar to pre-pandemic levels but rose from 15.0% to 17.5% going into fall 2021, with the largest increase among newly hired teachers.

readings.authors: Camp, A., Zamarro, G., & McGee, J. B.
readings.title: Changes in teachers' mobility and attrition in Arkansas during the first two years of the COVID-19 pandemic
readings.venue: EDRE Working Paper 2022-06, University of Arkansas
readings.note: Arkansas administrative data from 2018–19 through 2021–22 show teacher turnover held steady in the first pandemic year, then rose by about 2 percentage points (roughly 10%) in 2021–22, with variation across regions and by teacher and school characteristics.

readings.authors: Bastian, K. C., & Fuller, S. C.
readings.title: Educator attrition and hiring in North Carolina public schools during the COVID-19 pandemic
readings.note: Teacher attrition in North Carolina fell to 9.8% at the start of the pandemic, then rose to 15.6% by September 2022, when new hires fell short of departures by 1.8 percentage points for the first time in the period studied. Covers principals as well as teachers.

readings.authors: Feng, L., & Sass, T. R.
readings.title: The impact of incentives to recruit and retain teachers in “hard-to-staff” subjects
readings.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 37(1), 112–135
readings.note: Florida's loan forgiveness program reduced attrition among middle and high school math and science teachers by about 9–10%, and among special education teachers by 12% when fully funded. A one-time bonus reduced exits by as much as 32% in the short run.

readings.authors: Theobald, R., Xu, Z., Gilmour, A. F., Lachlan-Haché, L., Bettini, E., & Jones, N.
readings.title: The impact of a $10,000 bonus on special education teacher shortages in Hawaiʻi
readings.note: A $10,000 raise for special education teachers reduced the share of special education positions that were vacant, relative to general education, by about a third, almost entirely by drawing general education teachers into special education positions. Rare direct evidence on vacancies.

readings.authors: Clotfelter, C., Glennie, E., Ladd, H., & Vigdor, J.
readings.title: Would higher salaries keep teachers in high-poverty schools? Evidence from a policy intervention in North Carolina
readings.note: A $1,800 annual bonus for math, science and special education teachers in high-poverty or low-performing secondary schools reduced their turnover by about 17%, with the strongest response among experienced teachers.

readings.authors: Steele, J. L., Murnane, R. J., & Willett, J. B.
readings.title: Do financial incentives help low-performing schools attract and keep academically talented teachers? Evidence from California
readings.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 29(3), 451–478
readings.note: A competitively awarded $20,000 fellowship raised the probability that academically talented new teachers took jobs in low-performing schools by 28 percentage points. About three-quarters of both recipients and non-recipients who started in such schools stayed at least four years.

readings.authors: Hendricks, M. D.
readings.title: Does it pay to pay teachers more? Evidence from Texas
readings.note: Using Texas data, estimates that teacher turnover falls as pay rises (an elasticity of about −1.4), with the largest effects for inexperienced teachers and none after about 19 years of experience.
